content.p: For three years, from the summer of 1989 to the autumn of 1992, one of the most wanted men in Italy lived under a false name near Marseille. Domenico Libri, called "Don Mico", was a building contractor from Reggio Calabria whom police and magistrates described as the business arm of the city's 'Ndrangheta. When French and Italian agents took him at a Marseille airport on 16 September 1992, the Los Angeles Times counted him as the third of three fugitive bosses, from Sicily, Naples and Calabria, caught within ten days.

His story runs through the worst years of the Calabrian mafia's internal war. A sniper killed his son in a prison yard, another shot narrowly missed him outside a courthouse, and he slipped out of a hospital in Lombardy within minutes of eight carabinieri delivering him there. He then spent his last years as a sick old man in a flat in Tuscany, under sentences that the courts kept relaxing because of his health.

The Libri family controlled the Cannavò district of Reggio Calabria. Domenico and his brother Pasquale ran Edilizia Reggina, a firm that, according to la Repubblica in 1989, had monopolised billions of lire in subcontracts from the Gambogi company on the project to bury the railway line along the city's seafront. The newspaper said the brothers had started as foremen in the firm of the Cozzupoli family, Christian Democrats with weight in Reggio, and had later worked for themselves. The paper wrote in 1992 that even from compulsory residence in Milan he had managed to control a flow of large public contracts back home.

Prosecutors saw the brothers as the entrepreneurial wing of the city's clans. La Repubblica reported that the family built a fortified villa in Cannavò with sophisticated security systems, and that the Reggio court's preventive-measures section later confiscated movable and immovable property from them, the villa included, valued at six billion lire. A Gazzetta del Sud report of 2000 said the confiscation order for the villa had been served on the family some months before November 1991.

The Libris had always been allies of the De Stefano clan. When Paolo De Stefano was killed in October 1985, an event the newspapers tied to the outbreak of the war, Libri inherited much of the leadership of the allied clans, according to Reggio's prosecutors as reported in 1998. On the other side stood the Imerti-Condello grouping. The Observer later put the toll of that second war at about 600 lives in the six years to 1991. Other figures circulated at the time: la Repubblica spoke of 314 killings in Reggio and its province in 1987 and 1988 alone, and of almost 400 dead by June 1989, and in September 1992 it said the fighting had left almost a thousand dead in five years.

On 13 October 1986 Libri was arrested in Milan in a sweep ordered by the investigating magistrates Enzo Macrì and Vincenzo Lombardo, which la Repubblica described as the heaviest blow yet against the Reggio clans. He had been living in Milan under compulsory residence with Pasquale. He was now a defendant in a mass trial against the new clans, held in the high-security courtroom cages in Reggio, with almost a hundred defendants.

The war reached his family on a Sunday in September 1988. His son Pasquale Rocco Libri, 26, had been in prison for about a year. According to the reconstruction in la Repubblica, he was in cell 34 of the cellular wing of the old San Pietro prison, where the inmates from clans allied with the De Stefano were kept apart from the followers of the Imerti clan. He rarely left his cell, but that morning he was due to join other prisoners for a kickabout in the yard. A single shot, fired from the fifth-floor terrace of a building under construction about 150 metres away, hit him in the face. Investigators called the marksmanship Olympic standard and read the killing as a frontal assault on the brothers' business empire. Domenico and Pasquale themselves were then in prisons at Trani and Palmi.

The same reporting linked the sniper to two earlier episodes: a shot a year before that narrowly missed Antonio Libri, Pasquale Rocco's half-brother in that paper's account, and the killing of Francesco Zindato, described as a member of the clan. The date of the son's death is not settled: la Repubblica of 20 September 1988 places it on the preceding Sunday, a later article gives 10 September, and the Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission's 2003 report says July 1988.

On the morning of 17 March 1989, a little after nine, Libri arrived by ambulance from the Palmi prison for another hearing in the mass trial. On crutches because of an arterial disease of the legs, he was about to enter the rear door of the Palace of Justice when a shot was fired from a covered lorry parked about 200 metres away in via Mazzini. La Repubblica reported that the lorry had been stolen two days earlier and carried the plates of another stolen car, that two holes had been cut in its tarpaulin, one for the shooter and, it was believed, one for an accomplice watching the defendants arrive, and that the rifle was left behind on the vehicle. Libri apparently ducked. The expanding bullet passed close to him and lodged in the side of an armoured car assigned to one of the trial's magistrates.

Surrounded by carabinieri with sub-machine guns, he said, according to the paper, that the shot had been aimed not at him but at a judge. Police suspected the same sniper behind the son's death. Investigators reasoned that the Imerti-Condello side wanted to remove the Libris, who they believed had grown in importance within their alliance, in order to win the city.

In late May 1989 the Liberty Tribunal allowed Libri to be treated at a hospital in Busto Arsizio, in the Lombardy region, and, unusually, it did so without ordering that he be guarded. The magistrates who had sent the case to trial had already criticised the brothers' repeated stays in Reggio for supposed health reasons, when they should have been in confinement. Eight carabinieri took him north in an ambulance and followed in an armoured vehicle. In the early evening he was taken to the hospital's emergency room, where the escort left him. When the two doctors on duty came out of the operating theatre, he was gone.

The news reached the courtroom in Reggio just as a prosecutor was about to deliver his closing argument in the mass trial. The presiding judge Salvatore Boemi announced it. La Repubblica, citing police, said Libri left with the help of an accomplice and fled to avoid the snipers and to prepare a counter-offensive. Reports differ on the exact day: la Repubblica of 6 June 1989 put the escape on 2 June, while a 1992 piece in the same paper gave 5 June as the start of his life as a fugitive.

Police believed at first that he was in the north, among 'Ndrangheta families in Lombardy. In fact, la Repubblica reported in 1992, he had gone abroad almost at once and settled near Marseille with a false identity and new papers. The 1998 article said he had been managing huge investments there. In 1992 the paper reported that French police searched several homes of people he appeared to have met there; it did not report what they found.

The war went on without him. In the same paper's account, peace broke out in Reggio from November 1991 and the clans chose to recover strength and business rather than keep killing one another. The collaborator Paolo Iannò later told a Reggio court that the settlement was reached at a meeting of the main bosses in the mountains above Sinopoli.

The end came on the evening of Wednesday 16 September 1992, at about 7:15 pm, when Libri, 58, stepped off an Air Inter flight from Paris at a Marseille airport. Agents of Italy's SISDE and Interpol office had located him in Paris and worked with France's intelligence police, the Paris judicial police directorate and the regional judicial police in Marseille. Officers out of uniform served several international arrest warrants for mafia association and other charges. According to la Repubblica he was surprised, having believed himself safe, and offered no resistance. Italy's interior minister, Nicola Mancino, told the press, in the Los Angeles Times's words: "Finally, the fish are coming into the net."

La Repubblica said in 1998 that he was extradited about two years after his capture. By February of that year he had been convicted of mafia association and sentenced to twenty years, and had been declared a habitual offender. He was also accused of dozens of murders, and one of Boemi's colleagues had asked for a life sentence barely ten days before.

It was then that the Florence surveillance court, which had decided on 29 January to suspend the sentence because of what it called serious physical infirmity, sent him home. Boemi, now the anti-mafia prosecutor in Reggio, said his office learned of it after the fact. He called the decision an insult, in his words a slap in the face, to those who had worked to restore legality in Calabria (my translation of the Italian). He said Libri had once swapped medical records with another prisoner and had once escaped from a hospital, and that prosecutors doubted the illness. The paper described the former prisoner walking in the courtyard of his building in Reggio. Il Tirreno, looking back in 2006, told it differently: after surgery in September 1997 at a hospital in Prato, where the surgical ward was guarded for days by officers with sub-machine guns, a Florence surveillance judge decided in 1998 that his health was incompatible with prison and sent him to a house in Prato.

His son Antonio, himself among the thirty most dangerous fugitives in Italy and out of sight since November 1991, was caught on 23 May 2000. Gazzetta del Sud said police found him in his father-in-law's home in Reggio, in a hiding place behind a bookcase that opened as a moving wall. He had been sentenced to life in the first-instance Valanidi trial for several murders and to ten years for mafia association in the first Olimpia trial, in which he was acquitted of five other killings.

In December 2000 a Reggio court restored custody and Libri was taken to prison, but a surveillance judge in Messina soon returned him home on health grounds. In April 2002, Il Tirreno reported, police came to his flat in the centre of Prato to carry out a prison order after the sentence in the Olimpia trial became final. The paper said he was accused of 18 murders and had six life sentences at first instance. A board of experts appointed by the Reggio court again found him too ill, citing heart problems. People who knew him, the paper said, claimed that since his first trial in 1965 he had always complied with his reporting obligations and never tried to escape, a claim the 1989 hospital escape contradicts. The same court seized assets of 4 million euros from him: a company, five plots of land and several bank accounts.

In July 2005, the Florence surveillance judge extended his home detention until 2009. His lawyer, Costanza Malerba, had first defended him as a court-appointed counsel when he was held in the Pianosa maximum-security prison and had been his trusted lawyer for more than eight years. Il Tirreno wrote that people said he had ended up in Prato by chance, and in 2002 it had suggested he settled there because his trusted doctor lived in the city.

He died in the Secondigliano prison in Naples, aged 72, after an illness of long standing; the news was reported on 2 May 2006. Strill.it, a Reggio news site, wrote that, according to investigators and numerous court rulings, he had been for decades the undisputed head of the Reggio 'Ndrangheta clan that bore his name.

Libri's influence outlived him in court. In April 2010 Paolo Iannò, the former Condello-clan killer who became a collaborator in August 2002, testified by video link in Reggio in the "Testamento" trial of Libri's son Giuseppe and the businessman Bruno Crucitti. Iannò said Domenico Libri had been the leading figure of the clan allied with the De Stefano and Tegano families, active in Cannavò, Spirito Santo, San Cristoforo and central Reggio, and that he held the rank of "quartino", which Iannò described as the highest in the 'Ndrangheta. According to the witness, another son, Totò, had the rank of "vangelo", while Giuseppe managed the family's building firms. These are claims by one collaborator, tested in a court that was still sitting when the report was written.
